en: The *Preface to the Categorized Meaning of the Mahā-śamatha-vipaśyanā* contains Jingxi’s commentary on the three treatises and the essential meaning of the *Juntí*; however, it is particularly detailed regarding the factual matters in the *Fǔxíng*.

However, during Master Zhan’s time of composition, his days of lecturing were few; consequently, he was particularly deficient in the subtle art of organizing topical outlines (*kezhāng*) with meticulous and coherent linkage.

Later generations erroneously proclaimed that the Three Works of Jingxi must be strictly followed, treating the *Nian* (Commentary) as the basis for lecturing on the sutra and taking the headings of the *Ke* (Outlines) as their family tradition.
They went so far as to conjecture that the *Ke* were the *Zhù* (Commentary), and to stretch the *Zhù* into the *Ke*.

Forced interpretations and erroneous elaborations have caused the Patriarch’s intent to become obscured. In the past, the Elder of Tianxi took only the essential meaning of the Great Master’s teachings as his basis, establishing topical outlines for instruction;

thus, the textual principles became as clear as the sun rising over the earth. At that time, I maintained a private record, yet did not dare to compose a formal book, hoping instead for the Elder of Tianxi to finalize the topical divisions and bring them forth.
I never imagined that the Elder would pass away, leaving behind nothing but fragments of his words.

Both [volumes] are entrusted to the spirits of Bing and Ding. Now that the wise man has passed away, I fear these sacred texts may sink into oblivion. Therefore, during the course of my lectures, I have compiled what I had previously heard and integrated it with my own limited insights;
I have rearranged, added to, and subtracted from them to produce the *Zhiguan Ke* (Outline of Stopping and Contemplation) in two volumes, upper and lower, to bequeath to future worthies.

May this serve as a small contribution. As for the title "Guan Yi" (Penetrating the Meaning), it is intended solely so that the principles of stopping and contemplation may be interconnected and clearly illuminated, ensuring they do not remain buried.
They have merely sunk into the tangled undergrowth of commentators. Someone asked: "If that is so, then is this section specifically for the benefit of the wise?
I replied: "When I expound upon the Buddhist scriptures, I too simply present the principles of the sūtras to people.
I cannot follow the steps of Zhiyi’s commentaries by laboriously arranging headings at the beginning or fussing over his annotations."
Later, for the sake of propagating the sutras, I venture to call myself a contributing official of the Buddhas and Patriarchs;
I merely hope not to be a sinner who buries the essential principles of the Buddhas and Patriarchs beneath the feet of future generations.
Written on an autumn day in the year of Renxu by the Bhikṣu Lingyao, the fifth patriarch of the Tiantai teachings and contemplations, in the Dàshù Abbot’s Quarters at Lèngyán Jiǎngsì.
